topic: TILA, HOEPA and loan originator rules

notes.front: What is the Truth in Lending Act (TILA), and which regulation carries it out?
notes.back: The federal consumer-credit disclosure law at 15 U.S.C. 1601 and following; the Bureau's Regulation Z implements it.
notes.explanation: In Regulation Z, 'Act' means this statute, so every rule in the part rests on it.
notes.example: Like a food label for loans: before a home loan closes, the borrower sees its cost in a standard form.
notes.evidence: (1) Act means the Truth in Lending Act (15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.).

notes.front: Under Regulation Z, what is consumer credit?
notes.back: Credit offered or extended to a consumer primarily for personal, family or household purposes.
notes.explanation: The purpose of the credit, not the type of lender, decides whether it is consumer credit.
notes.example: Like a loan to buy the family home, but not a loan to buy a delivery van for a bakery.
notes.evidence: (12) Consumer credit means credit offered or extended to a consumer primarily for personal, family, or household purposes.

notes.front: Under Regulation Z, what is a dwelling?
notes.back: A residential structure with one to four units, attached to real property or not.
notes.explanation: Condominium and cooperative units, mobile homes and trailers count if used as a residence.
notes.example: Like a detached house, a duplex or a lived-in mobile home, but not a 20-flat apartment block.
notes.evidence: (19) Dwelling means a residential structure that contains one to four units, whether or not that structure is attached to real property. The term includes an individual condominium unit, cooperative unit, mobile home, and trailer, if it is used as a residence.

notes.front: What is a residential mortgage transaction?
notes.back: A transaction creating or retaining a mortgage or similar security interest in the consumer's principal dwelling to finance buying or first building it.
notes.explanation: The security interest may be a mortgage, deed of trust, installment-contract purchase money interest or an equivalent.
notes.example: Like the purchase loan a family takes out to buy the house they will live in.
notes.evidence: (24) Residential mortgage transaction means a transaction in which a mortgage, deed of trust, purchase money security interest arising under an installment sales contract, or equivalent consensual security interest is created or retained in the consumer's principal dwelling to finance the acquisition or initial construction of that dwelling.

notes.front: What is consummation?
notes.back: The time a consumer becomes contractually obligated on a credit transaction.
notes.explanation: Many Regulation Z deadlines, including the rescission clock, count from this moment.
notes.example: Like the moment a buyer signs the binding loan note at the closing table.
notes.evidence: (13) Consummation means the time that a consumer becomes contractually obligated on a credit transaction.

notes.front: Under Regulation Z's general rule, what is a business day?
notes.back: A day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for substantially all of its business functions.
notes.explanation: A more precise definition replaces this one for rescission and certain mortgage disclosures.
notes.example: Like counting only the days a bank branch is fully open, so a lender closed on Saturdays does not count Saturday.
notes.evidence: (6) Business day means a day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for carrying on substantially all of its business functions.

notes.front: What is the finance charge?
notes.back: The cost of consumer credit as a dollar amount: charges the consumer pays and the creditor imposes as an incident to or condition of credit.
notes.explanation: Charges of a type paid in a comparable cash transaction are left out.
notes.example: Like adding up interest, points and loan fees into one dollar figure for the loan.
notes.evidence: The finance charge is the cost of consumer credit as a dollar amount. It includes any charge payable directly or indirectly by the consumer and imposed directly or indirectly by the creditor as an incident to or a condition of the extension of credit. It does not include any charge of a type payable in a comparable cash transaction.

notes.front: What is the annual percentage rate (APR)?
notes.back: A yearly-rate measure of the cost of credit that relates the amount and timing of value received to payments made.
notes.explanation: It links what the consumer receives, and when, to what the consumer pays, and when.
notes.example: Like a price per kilo that lets you compare two different-sized packs, but for the yearly cost of two loans.
notes.evidence: The annual percentage rate is a measure of the cost of credit, expressed as a yearly rate, that relates the amount and timing of value received by the consumer to the amount and timing of payments made.

notes.front: What is the right of rescission?
notes.back: The right of each consumer whose ownership interest in their principal dwelling becomes subject to a security interest to cancel the credit transaction.
notes.explanation: Transactions listed in § 1026.23(f) do not carry the right.
notes.example: Like a cooling-off period on a doorstep sale, but for a loan that puts a lien on your home.
notes.evidence: In a credit transaction in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in a consumer's principal dwelling, each consumer whose ownership interest is or will be subject to the security interest shall have the right to rescind the transaction, except for transactions described in paragraph (f) of this section.

notes.front: In closed-end credit advertising, what are triggering terms?
notes.back: Terms that, if an advertisement states them, require it to give additional disclosures.
notes.explanation: They are listed in § 1026.24(d)(1), and the extra terms required are in § 1026.24(d)(2).
notes.example: Like a tripwire: mention one kind of detail and a set of extra disclosures must follow.
notes.evidence: Triggering terms. If any of the following terms is set forth in an advertisement, the advertisement shall meet the requirements of paragraph (d)(2) of this section:

notes.front: What is the Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act (HOEPA), and where is it implemented?
notes.back: A 1994 federal law, implemented in Regulation Z's § 1026.32, that covers high-cost mortgages.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z's § 1026.32(a) decides whether a loan is a high-cost mortgage under it.
notes.example: Like extra safety rules that switch on only for the most expensive home loans.
notes.evidence: For covered loans subject to the Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act of 1994, as implemented in Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.32, whether the covered loan is a high-cost mortgage under Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.32(a).
introduces: Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act
uses: Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act

notes.front: What is a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: A consumer credit transaction secured by the consumer's principal dwelling that exceeds an APR, points-and-fees or prepayment-penalty test in § 1026.32(a)(1).
notes.explanation: Some transactions are exempt under § 1026.32(a)(2).
notes.example: Like a home-equity loan priced so steeply that extra borrower protections switch on.
notes.evidence: The requirements of this section apply to a high-cost mortgage, which is any consumer credit transaction that is secured by the consumer's principal dwelling, other than as provided in paragraph (a)(2) of this section, and in which:

notes.front: What is the average prime offer rate (APOR)?
notes.back: An APR derived from average rates, points and other pricing currently offered by a representative sample of creditors for low-risk mortgages.
notes.explanation: It is built from rates, points and other pricing terms, not from the interest rate alone.
notes.example: Like a market benchmark price that a particular loan's APR is measured against.
notes.evidence: "Average prime offer rate" means an annual percentage rate that is derived from average interest rates, points, and other loan pricing terms currently offered to consumers by a representative sample of creditors for mortgage transactions that have low-risk pricing characteristics.

notes.front: What is a higher-priced mortgage loan (HPML)?
notes.back: A closed-end consumer credit loan secured by the consumer's principal dwelling whose APR exceeds the APOR by set margins.
notes.explanation: The comparison uses the APOR for a comparable transaction as of the date the interest rate is set.
notes.example: Like a speed camera: a loan priced far enough above the benchmark triggers extra rules.
notes.evidence: "Higher-priced mortgage loan" means a closed-end consumer credit transaction secured by the consumer's principal dwelling with an annual percentage rate that exceeds the average prime offer rate for a comparable transaction as of the date the interest rate is set:

notes.front: Under Regulation Z's § 1026.36, who is a loan originator?
notes.back: Someone who, for or expecting compensation, takes an application, offers, arranges, negotiates or otherwise obtains consumer credit for another person.
notes.explanation: Assisting a consumer in applying also counts, if done for pay or expected gain.
notes.example: Like a bank's mortgage officer or an independent broker who takes your application for a fee.
notes.evidence: means a person who, in expectation of direct or indirect compensation or other monetary gain or for direct or indirect compensation or other monetary gain, performs any of the following activities: takes an application, offers, arranges, assists a consumer in obtaining or applying to obtain, negotiates, or otherwise obtains or makes an extension of consumer credit for another person;

notes.front: In loan originator pay rules, what is a proxy for a term of a transaction?
notes.back: A factor that consistently varies with a term over many transactions and that the originator can add, drop or change.
notes.explanation: Both conditions must hold: consistent variation with the term, and the originator's power over the factor.
notes.example: Like paying a salesperson by which paperwork option they pick, when that option always travels with the pricier rate.
notes.evidence: A factor that is not itself a term of a transaction is a proxy for a term of the transaction if the factor consistently varies with that term over a significant number of transactions, and the loan originator has the ability, directly or indirectly, to add, drop, or change the factor in originating the transaction.

notes.front: What does the ban on dual compensation mean for a loan originator?
notes.back: If the consumer pays a loan originator directly, nobody else may pay a loan originator on that loan, except a firm paying its own staff.
notes.explanation: The ban stops a loan originator being paid twice for one loan. Section 1026.36(d)(2)(i)(C) still lets a consumer-paid firm pay its own individual loan originators, but not on the terms of the loan.
notes.example: Like a tradesperson paid by the homeowner who may not also take a fee from the supplier on the same job.
notes.evidence: (1) No loan originator shall receive compensation, directly or indirectly, from any person other than the consumer in connection with the transaction; and

notes.front: In Regulation Z, what is steering by a loan originator?
notes.back: Directing a consumer into a transaction because the originator gets more pay from the creditor for it, unless it is in the consumer's interest.
notes.explanation: The exception is a transaction that is in the consumer's interest.
notes.example: Like a waiter pushing the dish that earns him the biggest bonus, not the one that suits you.
notes.evidence: a loan originator shall not direct or "steer" a consumer to consummate a transaction based on the fact that the originator will receive greater compensation from the creditor in that transaction than in other transactions the originator offered or could have offered to the consumer, unless the consummated transaction is in the consumer's interest.

notes.front: What is the ability-to-repay (ATR) rule?
notes.back: A creditor must make a reasonable, good-faith determination, at or before consummation, that the consumer can repay the loan according to its terms.
notes.explanation: It applies to covered transactions; without that determination the loan may not be made.
notes.example: Like a landlord checking a tenant's income before signing, but required by law for home loans.
notes.evidence: A creditor shall not make a loan that is a covered transaction unless the creditor makes a reasonable and good faith determination at or before consummation that the consumer will have a reasonable ability to repay the loan according to its terms.

notes.front: What is a qualified mortgage (QM)?
notes.back: A loan meeting the rule's QM criteria, which gives the creditor a presumption that it complied with the ATR requirement.
notes.explanation: The presumption attaches loan by loan, when that loan meets the QM criteria.
notes.example: Like a pre-approved design that building inspectors presume is safe.
notes.evidence: the creditor is presumed to comply with the ATR requirement with regard to a particular loan the creditor originates if the loan satisfies the criteria to be a QM pursuant to the Rule.
notes.source: CFPB, Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage Rule: Small Entity Compliance Guide (version 3.1, April 2021), PDF page 13

notes.front: The purpose of Regulation Z is to promote the {{c1::informed use of consumer credit}} by requiring disclosures about its terms and cost.
notes.explanation: It also aims to give consumers more timely information on the costs of the residential real estate settlement process.
notes.evidence: The purpose of this part is to promote the informed use of consumer credit by requiring disclosures about its terms and cost, to ensure that consumers are provided with greater and more timely information on the nature and costs of the residential real estate settlement process,

notes.front: Besides disclosures, what substantive protection does Regulation Z give on credit that involves a lien on the consumer's principal dwelling?
notes.back: The right to cancel certain such credit transactions.
notes.explanation: The regulation also regulates certain credit card practices and billing disputes.
notes.evidence: The regulation also includes substantive protections. It gives consumers the right to cancel certain credit transactions that involve a lien on a consumer's principal dwelling, regulates certain credit card practices, and provides a means for fair and timely resolution of credit billing disputes.

notes.front: A sole trader borrows to buy equipment for her plumbing business. Is the loan subject to Regulation Z?
notes.back: No. Credit primarily for a business, commercial or agricultural purpose is exempt.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z covers consumer credit, which serves personal, family or household purposes.
notes.evidence: (1) An extension of credit primarily for a business, commercial or agricultural purpose.

notes.front: Is credit extended to a corporation or a government agency subject to Regulation Z?
notes.back: No. Credit to other than a natural person is exempt.
notes.explanation: The exemption expressly includes government agencies and instrumentalities.
notes.evidence: (2) An extension of credit to other than a natural person, including credit to government agencies or instrumentalities.

notes.front: A consumer loan exceeds the annual threshold amount but is secured by real property. Does the large-credit exemption apply?
notes.back: No. The exemption does not cover credit secured by real property or by personal property used as the consumer's principal dwelling.
notes.explanation: A large loan secured by a home therefore stays inside Regulation Z.
notes.evidence: (A) Secured by any real property, or by personal property used or expected to be used as the principal dwelling of the consumer; or

notes.front: What test decides whether credit to a natural person is consumer credit?
notes.back: Whether it is primarily for personal, family or household purposes.
notes.explanation: The word 'primarily' means the main purpose governs, so a loan used mainly for business falls outside.
notes.evidence: (12) Consumer credit means credit offered or extended to a consumer primarily for personal, family, or household purposes.

notes.front: A consumer takes a loan secured by her lakeside holiday cottage. Is the cottage a dwelling for Regulation Z?
notes.back: Yes. A dwelling need not be the principal residence, so a vacation or second home can be a dwelling.
notes.explanation: The principal-residence limit applies only for residential mortgage transactions and rescission.
notes.evidence: A dwelling need not be the consumer's principal residence to fit the definition, and thus a vacation or second home could be a dwelling.

notes.front: Is a residential building with five units a dwelling under Regulation Z?
notes.back: No. A dwelling contains one to four units.
notes.explanation: Five or more units takes the structure outside the definition.
notes.evidence: (19) Dwelling means a residential structure that contains one to four units, whether or not that structure is attached to real property.

notes.front: For a residential mortgage transaction, must the dwelling be the consumer's principal residence?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: The same principal-residence limit applies to the right to rescind.
notes.evidence: However, for purposes of the definition of residential mortgage transaction and the right to rescind, a dwelling must be the principal residence of the consumer.

notes.front: A homeowner who bought her house years ago takes a home-equity loan on it to pay for a car. Is this a residential mortgage transaction?
notes.back: No. The loan does not finance the acquisition or initial construction of the dwelling.
notes.explanation: Only financing to buy or first build the principal dwelling qualifies.
notes.evidence: is created or retained in the consumer's principal dwelling to finance the acquisition or initial construction of that dwelling.

notes.front: Which law decides when a consumer becomes contractually obligated, and so when consummation occurs?
notes.back: Applicable state law; Regulation Z does not make that determination.
notes.explanation: A commitment agreement that binds the consumer under that law, for example, would be consummation.
notes.evidence: When a contractual obligation on the consumer's part is created is a matter to be determined under applicable law; Regulation Z does not make this determination.

notes.front: A consumer pays a nonrefundable application fee. Has consummation occurred?
notes.back: No, not merely because of that payment, unless applicable law holds otherwise.
notes.explanation: A financial investment in the transaction is not the same as becoming contractually obligated.
notes.evidence: Consummation, however, does not occur merely because the consumer has made some financial investment in the transaction (for example, by paying a nonrefundable fee) unless, of course, applicable law holds otherwise.

notes.front: For rescission and certain mortgage disclosures, what is a business day?
notes.back: Every calendar day except Sundays and the federal legal public holidays.
notes.explanation: Saturdays count under this precise rule even if the creditor's office is closed.
notes.evidence: the term means all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a),

notes.front: Can you name two of the legal public holidays excluded from the precise business-day count?
notes.back: Any two of: New Year's Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day (among others).
notes.explanation: The list follows 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) and also includes Memorial Day and Veterans Day, among others.
notes.evidence: such as New Year's Day, the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr., Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving Day, and Christmas Day.

notes.front: How do Regulation Z's two definitions of 'business day' differ?
notes.back: General: days the creditor's offices are open for substantially all business. Precise: all calendar days except Sundays and federal legal public holidays.
notes.explanation: The precise rule governs rescission and certain mortgage disclosure timings; the general rule governs the rest.
notes.contrast: A lender closed on Saturdays does not count Saturday under the general rule, but Saturday counts under the precise rule.
notes.evidence: However, for purposes of rescission under §§ 1026.15 and 1026.23,

notes.front: When is a fee charged by a third party part of the finance charge?
notes.back: When the creditor requires use of the third party as a condition of or incident to the credit, even if the consumer chooses which one.
notes.explanation: The consumer's freedom to pick the provider does not take the fee out.
notes.evidence: (i) Requires the use of a third party as a condition of or an incident to the extension of credit, even if the consumer can choose the third party; or

notes.front: A consumer pays a mortgage broker's fee directly to the broker; the creditor did not require a broker and keeps none of the fee. Is it a finance charge?
notes.back: Yes. Mortgage broker fees are finance charges even then.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z makes a special rule for broker fees, whoever collects them.
notes.evidence: Fees charged by a mortgage broker (including fees paid by the consumer directly to the broker or to the creditor for delivery to the broker) are finance charges even if the creditor does not require the consumer to use a mortgage broker and even if the creditor does not retain any portion of the charge.

notes.front: Points, loan fees, assumption fees, {{c1::finder's fees}} and similar charges are examples of finance charges.
notes.explanation: They fall under § 1026.4(b)(3) unless a specific exclusion applies.
notes.evidence: (3) Points, loan fees, assumption fees, finder's fees, and similar charges.

notes.front: A lender charges every applicant a $75 application fee, whether or not the loan is made. Is the fee a finance charge?
notes.back: No. Application fees charged to all applicants are excluded.
notes.explanation: The exclusion depends on the fee being charged to all applicants, win or lose.
notes.evidence: (1) Application fees charged to all applicants for credit, whether or not credit is actually extended.

notes.front: Are charges for actual, unanticipated late payment part of the finance charge?
notes.back: No. They are excluded.
notes.explanation: Charges for exceeding a credit limit, delinquency or default are excluded on the same footing.
notes.evidence: (2) Charges for actual unanticipated late payment, for exceeding a credit limit, or for delinquency, default, or a similar occurrence.

notes.front: Are seller's points part of the buyer's finance charge?
notes.back: No. Seller's points are excluded from the finance charge.
notes.explanation: Seller's points are item (5) on that list of excluded charges.
notes.evidence: The following charges are not finance charges:

notes.front: In a residential mortgage transaction, when are real-estate related fees such as title fees excluded from the finance charge?
notes.back: When they are bona fide and reasonable in amount.
notes.explanation: The exclusion covers transactions secured by real property as well as residential mortgage transactions.
notes.evidence: (7) Real-estate related fees. The following fees in a transaction secured by real property or in a residential mortgage transaction, if the fees are bona fide and reasonable in amount:

notes.front: Which two methods may be used to determine the APR?
notes.back: The actuarial method or the United States Rule method.
notes.explanation: Appendix J gives the equations and instructions for the actuarial method.
notes.evidence: The annual percentage rate shall be determined in accordance with either the actuarial method or the United States Rule method. Explanations, equations and instructions for determining the annual percentage rate in accordance with the actuarial method are set forth in appendix J to this part.

notes.front: As a general rule, a disclosed APR is accurate if it is within {{c1::1/8 of 1 percentage point}} of the correctly determined APR.
notes.explanation: The margin applies above or below the correct rate.
notes.evidence: As a general rule, the annual percentage rate shall be considered accurate if it is not more than 1/8 of 1 percentage point above or below the annual percentage rate determined in accordance with paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

notes.front: A lender discloses an APR of 6.60% on a loan with a regular payment schedule; the correctly computed APR is 6.70%. Is the disclosed APR accurate?
notes.back: Yes. The difference is 0.10 of a point, within the general 1/8-point (0.125) tolerance.
notes.explanation: The tolerance applies whether the disclosed rate is above or below the correct one.
notes.evidence: As a general rule, the annual percentage rate shall be considered accurate if it is not more than 1/8 of 1 percentage point above or below the annual percentage rate determined in accordance with paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

notes.front: What APR tolerance applies to an irregular transaction, such as one with multiple advances?
notes.back: 1/4 of 1 percentage point above or below the correct APR.
notes.explanation: It is twice the general 1/8-point tolerance.
notes.evidence: In an irregular transaction, the annual percentage rate shall be considered accurate if it is not more than 1/4 of 1 percentage point above or below the annual percentage rate determined in accordance with paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

notes.front: How does a mortgage's APR differ from its interest rate?
notes.back: The interest rate is the yearly cost of borrowing the money; the APR is broader, adding points, broker fees and other charges.
notes.explanation: Because the APR adds those costs, it is usually higher than the interest rate.
notes.contrast: Interest rate: the price of the money. APR: the price of the money plus the cost of getting it.
notes.evidence: The APR reflects the interest rate, any points, mortgage broker fees, and other charges that you pay to get the loan. For that reason, your APR is usually higher than your interest rate.
notes.source: CFPB, Ask CFPB: “What is the difference between a mortgage interest rate and an APR?”

notes.front: Does a mortgage's interest rate reflect fees and other charges?
notes.back: No. It is the yearly cost of borrowing the money, as a percentage, without fees or other charges.
notes.explanation: Fees and points show up in the APR instead.
notes.evidence: The interest rate is the cost you will pay each year to borrow the money, expressed as a percentage rate. It does not reflect fees or any other charges you may have to pay for the loan.
notes.source: CFPB, Ask CFPB: “What is the difference between a mortgage interest rate and an APR?”

notes.front: A borrower compares two adjustable-rate loans by APR alone. What limit of the APR should she know?
notes.back: For adjustable-rate loans, the APR does not reflect the loan's maximum interest rate.
notes.explanation: The consumer page advises taking care when comparing APRs of adjustable-rate loans.
notes.evidence: Take care when comparing the APRs of adjustable-rate mortgage loans. For adjustable rate mortgage loans, the APR does not reflect the maximum interest rate of the loan.
notes.source: CFPB, Ask CFPB: “What is the difference between a mortgage interest rate and an APR?”

notes.front: How does a consumer exercise the right to rescind, and when is notice treated as given?
notes.back: By written notice to the creditor; it counts as given when mailed, or when delivered if sent another way.
notes.explanation: Mail, telegram or other written communication all qualify.
notes.evidence: To exercise the right to rescind, the consumer shall notify the creditor of the rescission by mail, telegram or other means of written communication. Notice is considered given when mailed,

notes.front: Two co-owners share a home-equity loan subject to rescission. Only one sends a rescission notice. What is the effect?
notes.back: The rescission is effective as to all consumers in the transaction.
notes.explanation: When several consumers hold the right, any one of them can exercise it for everyone.
notes.evidence: When more than one consumer in a transaction has the right to rescind, the exercise of the right by one consumer shall be effective as to all consumers.

notes.front: How many copies of the notice of the right to rescind must each consumer entitled to rescind receive?
notes.back: Two copies each.
notes.explanation: Each consumer entitled to rescind gets their own two copies.
notes.evidence: a creditor shall deliver two copies of the notice of the right to rescind to each consumer entitled to rescind

notes.front: Unless the right is waived, what must the creditor hold back until the rescission period ends?
notes.back: Disbursing money (other than in escrow), performing services and delivering materials.
notes.explanation: It must also be reasonably satisfied that the consumer has not rescinded.
notes.evidence: no money shall be disbursed other than in escrow, no services shall be performed and no materials delivered until the rescission period has expired and the creditor is reasonably satisfied that the consumer has not rescinded.

notes.front: The consumer may rescind until midnight of the {{c1::third business day}} after consummation, delivery of the rescission notice, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever is last.
notes.explanation: The latest of the three events starts the clock.
notes.evidence: The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last.

notes.front: A home-equity loan on a principal dwelling closes on a Friday, with the notice and all material disclosures given at closing. No holidays fall in the next week. When does the right to rescind end?
notes.choices:
A) Midnight on Monday
B) Midnight on Tuesday
C) Midnight on Wednesday
D) At the end of the following Friday
notes.back: B) Midnight on Tuesday.
notes.explanation: Under the precise business-day rule, Saturday counts and Sunday does not, so Saturday, Monday and Tuesday are the three business days.
notes.choicesExplained: A counts Sunday, which is never a business day for rescission. C wrongly drops Saturday, which counts under the precise rule. D has no basis: the right lasts three business days, not a week.
notes.evidence: The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation,

notes.front: If the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered, the right to rescind expires {{c1::3 years}} after consummation, or sooner on transfer or sale of the property.
notes.explanation: Whichever of those events comes first ends the extended right.
notes.evidence: If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first.

notes.front: A creditor never delivered the rescission notice. Eighteen months later the consumer sells the house. Can she still rescind?
notes.back: No. The extended right ends on sale of the property, even before 3 years.
notes.explanation: The right expires at 3 years, transfer of all interest, or sale, whichever comes first.
notes.evidence: the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first.

notes.front: Can you name two of the 'material disclosures' whose non-delivery extends the rescission right?
notes.back: Any two of: the APR, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule.
notes.explanation: Failing to deliver any of them keeps the right open for up to 3 years.
notes.evidence: the term "material disclosures" means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule,

notes.front: A family takes a loan to buy the house they will live in, secured by that house. Do they get a right of rescission?
notes.back: No. A residential mortgage transaction is exempt.
notes.explanation: Purchase-money loans for the principal dwelling are the first listed exemption.
notes.evidence: (1) A residential mortgage transaction.

notes.front: A homeowner refinances with her existing lender and takes $20,000 in new cash. Does any right of rescission apply?
notes.back: Yes, but only to the new money above the unpaid balance, earned finance charges and refinancing costs.
notes.explanation: A same-creditor refinance is otherwise exempt.
notes.evidence: The right of rescission shall apply, however, to the extent the new amount financed exceeds the unpaid principal balance, any earned unpaid finance charge on the existing debt, and amounts attributed solely to the costs of the refinancing or consolidation.

notes.front: Is a refinancing by the same creditor of credit already secured by the consumer's principal dwelling subject to rescission?
notes.back: No, apart from any new money advanced.
notes.explanation: The exemption covers a refinancing or consolidation by the same creditor.
notes.evidence: (2) A refinancing or consolidation by the same creditor of an extension of credit already secured by the consumer's principal dwelling.

notes.front: Is a transaction in which a state agency is the creditor subject to rescission?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: It is one of the listed exempt transactions in § 1026.23(f).
notes.evidence: (3) A transaction in which a state agency is a creditor.

notes.front: When a consumer rescinds, what happens to the security interest and to the finance charge?
notes.back: The security interest becomes void, and the consumer is not liable for any amount, including any finance charge.
notes.explanation: Voiding the security interest removes the lien that gave rise to the right.
notes.evidence: When a consumer rescinds a transaction, the security interest giving rise to the right of rescission becomes void and the consumer shall not be liable for any amount, including any finance charge.

notes.front: How does a consumer facing a bona fide personal financial emergency waive the right to rescind?
notes.back: By a dated written statement describing the emergency, waiving the right, and signed by all consumers entitled to rescind.
notes.explanation: Printed forms for this purpose are prohibited.
notes.evidence: To modify or waive the right, the consumer shall give the creditor a dated written statement that describes the emergency, specifically modifies or waives the right to rescind, and bears the signature of all the consumers entitled to rescind. Printed forms for this purpose are prohibited.

notes.front: Is stating the amount or percentage of a down payment in a closed-end credit advertisement a triggering term?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: It is the first item in the § 1026.24(d)(1) list.
notes.evidence: (i) The amount or percentage of any downpayment.

notes.front: Which triggering term concerns how long the consumer will be paying?
notes.back: The number of payments or the period of repayment.
notes.explanation: An advert saying '30-year loan' or '360 payments' states this term.
notes.evidence: (ii) The number of payments or period of repayment.

notes.front: Which triggering term concerns what each instalment costs?
notes.back: The amount of any payment.
notes.explanation: An advert quoting a monthly payment figure states this term.
notes.evidence: (iii) The amount of any payment.

notes.front: Which triggering term concerns the dollar cost of the credit?
notes.back: The amount of any finance charge.
notes.explanation: It is the fourth item in the § 1026.24(d)(1) list.
notes.evidence: (iv) The amount of any finance charge.

notes.front: An advertisement for a home loan says only: 'Just $1,450 a month!' What else must it state?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more, since a payment is not a triggering term
B) Only the interest rate
C) The down payment, the terms of repayment, and the 'annual percentage rate', using that term
D) The lender's licence number only
notes.back: C) The down payment, the terms of repayment, and the 'annual percentage rate', using that term.
notes.explanation: A payment amount is a triggering term, so the advertisement must give the § 1026.24(d)(2) terms, as applicable.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the amount of a payment is a triggering term. B omits the required APR and other terms. D is not what § 1026.24(d)(2) requires.
notes.evidence: (iii) The "annual percentage rate," using that term, and, if the rate may be increased after consummation, that fact.

notes.front: What rule governs specific credit terms stated in an advertisement?
notes.back: It may state only terms that actually are or will be arranged or offered by the creditor.
notes.explanation: A creditor may not advertise a rate it is not prepared to offer.
notes.evidence: If an advertisement for credit states specific credit terms, it shall state only those terms that actually are or will be arranged or offered by the creditor.

notes.front: A first-lien transaction is a high-cost mortgage if its APR will exceed the APOR for a comparable transaction by more than {{c1::6.5}} percentage points.
notes.explanation: The margin is measured against the APOR for a comparable transaction.
notes.evidence: (A) 6.5 percentage points for a first-lien transaction, other than as described in paragraph (a)(1)(i)(B) of this section;

notes.front: What APR trigger over APOR makes a subordinate-lien transaction a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: More than 8.5 percentage points.
notes.explanation: Subordinate liens get a wider margin than most first liens.
notes.evidence: (C) 8.5 percentage points for a subordinate-lien transaction; or

notes.front: A first-lien loan on a site-built house has an APR 7.0 percentage points above the APOR for a comparable transaction. Points, fees and prepayment terms are within limits. Is it a high-cost mortgage?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because 7.0 exceeds the 6.5-point first-lien trigger
B) No, because the first-lien trigger is 8.5 points
C) No, because points and fees are within limits
D) Only if it is also a subordinate lien
notes.back: A) Yes, because 7.0 exceeds the 6.5-point first-lien trigger.
notes.explanation: 7.0 points is above the 6.5-point first-lien margin.
notes.choicesExplained: B applies 8.5, which is for subordinate liens or small personal-property loans. C is wrong: the tests are alternatives. D confuses the lien types.
notes.evidence: (A) 6.5 percentage points for a first-lien transaction, other than as described in paragraph (a)(1)(i)(B) of this section;

notes.front: For a loan amount of $20,000 or more (adjusted annually), a transaction is a high-cost mortgage if total points and fees exceed {{c1::5 percent}} of the total loan amount.
notes.explanation: The $20,000 figure is adjusted every year on January 1.
notes.evidence: (A) 5 percent of the total loan amount for a transaction with a loan amount of $20,000 or more; the $20,000 figure shall be adjusted annually on January 1

notes.front: For a loan under $20,000 (adjusted annually), what points-and-fees level makes it a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: Points and fees above the lesser of 8 percent of the total loan amount or $1,000 (adjusted annually).
notes.explanation: The lower of the two limits is the one that applies.
notes.evidence: (B) The lesser of 8 percent of the total loan amount or $1,000 for a transaction with a loan amount of less than $20,000;

notes.front: A $200,000 first-lien home loan (above the indexed $20,000 threshold) has $11,000 in total points and fees, and its APR is within limits. Is it a high-cost mortgage?
notes.choices:
A) Yes. $11,000 is 5.5 percent of the loan, above the 5 percent points-and-fees trigger
B) No, because the APR is within limits
C) No, because the points-and-fees trigger is 8 percent
D) No, because the trigger is a flat $1,000
notes.back: A) Yes. $11,000 is 5.5 percent of the loan, above the 5 percent points-and-fees trigger.
notes.explanation: 5 percent of $200,000 is $10,000, and the loan's points and fees exceed that.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the points-and-fees test works on its own. C and D state the test for loans under $20,000, not this loan.
notes.evidence: (A) 5 percent of the total loan amount for a transaction with a loan amount of $20,000 or more;

notes.front: Which prepayment-penalty terms make a loan a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: A penalty chargeable more than 36 months after consummation or account opening, or penalties that can exceed 2 percent of the amount prepaid.
notes.explanation: Either feature alone is enough.
notes.evidence: the creditor can charge a prepayment penalty, as defined in paragraph (b)(6) of this section, more than 36 months after consummation or account opening, or prepayment penalties that can exceed, in total, more than 2 percent of the amount prepaid.

notes.front: A home loan lets the creditor charge a 1 percent prepayment penalty during the first four years. Is it a high-cost mortgage under the prepayment test?
notes.back: Yes. The penalty can be charged more than 36 months after consummation.
notes.explanation: The amount is under 2 percent, but the period test is failed on its own.
notes.evidence: the creditor can charge a prepayment penalty, as defined in paragraph (b)(6) of this section, more than 36 months after consummation or account opening,

notes.front: Is a transaction to finance the initial construction of a dwelling subject to the high-cost mortgage rules?
notes.back: No. It is exempt.
notes.explanation: It is one of four exemptions listed in § 1026.32(a)(2).
notes.evidence: (ii) A transaction to finance the initial construction of a dwelling;

notes.front: What balloon payment does § 1026.32(d) generally bar in a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: A scheduled payment more than two times a regular periodic payment.
notes.explanation: Exceptions exist, such as schedules adjusted to seasonal or irregular income.
notes.evidence: (i) Balloon payment. Except as provided by paragraphs (d)(1)(ii) and (iii) of this section, a payment schedule with a payment that is more than two times a regular periodic payment.

notes.front: May a high-cost mortgage have regular payments that make the principal balance grow?
notes.back: No. Negative amortisation is barred.
notes.explanation: It is a listed prohibited term in § 1026.32(d)(2).
notes.evidence: (2) Negative amortization. A payment schedule with regular periodic payments that cause the principal balance to increase.

notes.front: May a high-cost mortgage raise the interest rate after the borrower defaults?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: An increase in the interest rate after default is a prohibited term.
notes.evidence: (4) Increased interest rate. An increase in the interest rate after default.

notes.front: A loan is a high-cost mortgage. Which term may it lawfully include?
notes.choices:
A) A prepayment penalty
B) Three periodic payments taken in advance from the proceeds
C) An interest rate that rises after default
D) Acceleration if the consumer commits fraud or material misrepresentation in connection with the loan
notes.back: D) Acceleration if the consumer commits fraud or material misrepresentation in connection with the loan.
notes.explanation: Acceleration is barred except in listed cases, one of which is fraud or material misrepresentation by the consumer.
notes.choicesExplained: A is barred outright. B is barred: more than two periodic payments may not be consolidated and paid in advance from the proceeds. C is barred.
notes.evidence: (i) There is fraud or material misrepresentation by the consumer in connection with the loan or open-end credit agreement;

notes.front: What must a creditor receive before it may extend a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: Written certification that the consumer got counselling on the mortgage's advisability from an approved counsellor.
notes.explanation: The counsellor must be approved by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development.
notes.evidence: A creditor shall not extend a high-cost mortgage to a consumer unless the creditor receives written certification that the consumer has obtained counseling on the advisability of the mortgage from a counselor that is approved to provide such counseling by the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

notes.front: A lender offers to have its own in-house counsellor provide the required high-cost mortgage counselling. Allowed?
notes.back: No. The counsellor may not be employed by or affiliated with the creditor.
notes.explanation: Independence from the creditor is a condition of valid counselling.
notes.evidence: The counseling required under this paragraph (a)(5) shall not be provided by a counselor who is employed by or affiliated with the creditor.

notes.front: May a creditor pay the counsellor's fees for high-cost mortgage counselling?
notes.back: Yes, but it may not make payment depend on the loan being consummated.
notes.explanation: The fee must be payable whether or not the mortgage goes ahead.
notes.evidence: A creditor may pay the fees of a counselor or counseling organization for providing counseling required under this paragraph (a)(5) but may not condition the payment of such fees on the consummation or account-opening of a mortgage transaction.

notes.front: How often does the Bureau update its table of average prime offer rates?
notes.back: At least weekly.
notes.explanation: The Bureau publishes the method it uses to derive the rates as well.
notes.evidence: The Bureau publishes average prime offer rates for a broad range of types of transactions in a table updated at least weekly as well as the methodology the Bureau uses to derive these rates.

notes.front: A creditor sets the interest rate on a first-lien home loan on 3 March and closes on 28 March. Which APOR should it compare the APR with for the HPML test?
notes.back: The APOR for a comparable transaction as of 3 March, the date the interest rate is set.
notes.explanation: The comparison date is when the rate is set, not the closing date.
notes.evidence: with an annual percentage rate that exceeds the average prime offer rate for a comparable transaction as of the date the interest rate is set:

notes.front: A home-equity line of credit on a principal dwelling is priced well above APOR. Can it be a higher-priced mortgage loan?
notes.back: No. The HPML definition covers only closed-end consumer credit.
notes.explanation: Open-end lines of credit fall outside the definition however they are priced.
notes.evidence: "Higher-priced mortgage loan" means a closed-end consumer credit transaction secured by the consumer's principal dwelling

notes.front: A first-lien loan within the Freddie Mac purchase limit is higher-priced if its APR exceeds APOR by {{c1::1.5}} or more percentage points.
notes.explanation: The limit is the maximum principal obligation eligible for purchase by Freddie Mac on the date the rate is set.
notes.evidence: (i) By 1.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a first lien with a principal obligation at consummation that does not exceed the limit in effect as of the date the transaction's interest rate is set for the maximum principal obligation eligible for purchase by Freddie Mac;

notes.front: A first-lien loan above the Freddie Mac purchase limit is higher-priced if its APR exceeds APOR by {{c1::2.5}} or more percentage points.
notes.explanation: Loans above that limit get a wider margin than those within it.
notes.evidence: (ii) By 2.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a first lien with a principal obligation at consummation that exceeds the limit in effect as of the date the transaction's interest rate is set for the maximum principal obligation eligible for purchase by Freddie Mac; or

notes.front: A subordinate-lien loan is higher-priced if its APR exceeds APOR by {{c1::3.5}} or more percentage points.
notes.explanation: Subordinate liens get a 3.5-point margin, wider than for first liens.
notes.evidence: (iii) By 3.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a subordinate lien.

notes.front: A closed-end second mortgage on a principal dwelling has an APR 3.0 percentage points above APOR. Is it a higher-priced mortgage loan?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because it is more than 1.5 points over APOR
B) No. A subordinate lien needs 3.5 or more points over APOR
C) Yes, because it is more than 2.5 points over APOR
D) No, because second mortgages are never higher-priced
notes.back: B) No. A subordinate lien needs 3.5 or more points over APOR.
notes.explanation: The 1.5-point test applies only to first liens within the Freddie Mac limit.
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the first-lien test. C applies the test for first liens above the Freddie Mac limit. D is wrong: subordinate liens can be higher-priced at 3.5 points or more.
notes.evidence: (iii) By 3.5 or more percentage points for loans secured by a subordinate lien.

notes.front: What must be in place before consummation of a first-lien higher-priced mortgage loan on a principal dwelling?
notes.back: An escrow account for property taxes and creditor-required mortgage-related insurance.
notes.explanation: The account must be set up before consummation, not afterwards.
notes.evidence: a creditor may not extend a higher-priced mortgage loan secured by a first lien on a consumer's principal dwelling unless an escrow account is established before consummation for payment of property taxes and premiums for mortgage-related insurance required by the creditor,

notes.front: After originating a first-lien higher-priced mortgage loan on a principal dwelling, the creditor must keep the escrow account for at least {{c1::five years}}.
notes.explanation: The Bureau's guide says this applies regardless of loan-to-value ratio.
notes.evidence: you must establish and maintain an escrow account for at least five years regardless of loan-to-value ratio.
notes.source: CFPB, TILA Higher-Priced Mortgage Loans Escrow Rule: Small Entity Compliance Guide (January 2021), PDF page 7

notes.front: Six years after closing, a borrower with a first-lien HPML asks to cancel her escrow account. She owes 85% of the original property value and is current. May the servicer cancel it?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because five years have passed
B) Yes, because she is current
C) No. The unpaid balance must be under 80 percent of the original value
D) No, the escrow can never be cancelled while the loan exists
notes.back: C) No. The unpaid balance must be under 80 percent of the original value.
notes.explanation: A request after five years allows cancellation only if the balance is below 80 percent of original value and the consumer is not delinquent or in default.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are true of her, but they are not enough: her balance is still above 80 percent of the original value. D is wrong: the escrow can be cancelled on request once every condition is met.
notes.evidence: (A) The unpaid principal balance is less than 80 percent of the original value of the property securing the underlying debt obligation; and

notes.front: Must an escrow account be set up for a higher-priced bridge loan with a term of twelve months or less?
notes.back: No. Such temporary or bridge loans are exempt.
notes.explanation: The exemption is one of several listed in § 1026.35(b)(2)(i).
notes.evidence: (C) A temporary or "bridge" loan with a loan term of twelve months or less,

notes.front: What appraisal does Regulation Z require before consummation of a higher-priced mortgage loan?
notes.back: A written appraisal by a certified or licensed appraiser who physically visits the property's interior.
notes.explanation: The appraiser must physically visit the interior, so a drive-by or desktop valuation will not do. Some loans are exempt under § 1026.35(c)(2), including qualified mortgages.
notes.evidence: The appraisal must be performed by a certified or licensed appraiser who conducts a physical visit of the interior of the property that will secure the transaction.

notes.front: A seller bought a house 60 days ago and is reselling it for 15 percent more to a buyer using an HPML. What appraisal rule applies?
notes.back: The creditor must obtain two written appraisals before consummation.
notes.explanation: Resale within 90 days at more than 10 percent above the seller's price triggers the second appraisal.
notes.evidence: (A) The seller acquired the property 90 or fewer days prior to the date of the consumer's agreement to acquire the property and the price in the consumer's agreement to acquire the property exceeds the seller's acquisition price by more than 10 percent; or

notes.front: A processor only gathers documents and orders records for the loan officer; she never takes applications or discusses terms. Is she a loan originator?
notes.back: No. Purely administrative or clerical tasks for someone who originates are excluded.
notes.explanation: The exclusion requires that she neither take applications nor offer or negotiate terms.
notes.evidence: (A) A person who does not take a consumer credit application or offer or negotiate credit terms available from a creditor, but who performs purely administrative or clerical tasks on behalf of a person who does engage in such activities.

notes.front: For § 1026.36, who is a mortgage broker in a particular transaction?
notes.back: Any loan originator who is not an employee of the creditor.
notes.explanation: Regulation Z builds this definition on its broader loan originator definition.
notes.evidence: (2) Mortgage broker. For purposes of this section, a mortgage broker with respect to a particular transaction is any loan originator that is not an employee of the creditor.

notes.front: In § 1026.36, what does 'compensation' include?
notes.back: Salaries, commissions, and any financial or similar incentive.
notes.explanation: The term is wide, so bonuses and similar rewards count too.
notes.evidence: (3) Compensation. The term "compensation" includes salaries, commissions, and any financial or similar incentive.

notes.front: On dwelling-secured consumer credit, what may a loan originator's pay not be based on?
notes.back: A term of the transaction, or the terms of multiple transactions.
notes.explanation: The ban runs both ways: on receiving and on paying such compensation.
notes.evidence: no loan originator shall receive and no person shall pay to a loan originator, directly or indirectly, compensation in an amount that is based on a term of a transaction, the terms of multiple transactions by an individual loan originator,

notes.front: For the loan originator pay rule, what is a 'term of a transaction'?
notes.back: Any right or obligation of the parties to a credit transaction.
notes.explanation: The definition is broad, reaching well beyond the interest rate.
notes.evidence: For purposes of this paragraph (d)(1) only, a "term of a transaction" is any right or obligation of the parties to a credit transaction.

notes.front: A loan officer is paid 1 percent of every loan amount she closes, with a minimum and maximum dollar cap. Is that pay based on a term of the transaction?
notes.back: No. A fixed percentage of the amount of credit is allowed, and may have a minimum or maximum.
notes.explanation: The amount of credit is not treated as a term, or proxy for a term, when pay is a fixed percentage of it.
notes.evidence: The amount of credit extended is not a term of a transaction or a proxy for a term of a transaction, provided that compensation received by or paid to a loan originator, directly or indirectly, is based on a fixed percentage of the amount of credit extended;

notes.front: A lender pays its loan officers an extra 0.5 percent of the loan amount on any loan closed at a rate above its daily rate sheet. What is the problem?
notes.choices:
A) None, if the bonus is disclosed to the consumer
B) The pay is based on a term of the transaction, the interest rate, which § 1026.36(d)(1) forbids
C) None, because the bonus is a percentage of the loan amount
D) It is only a problem for mortgage brokers, not employees
notes.back: B) The pay is based on a term of the transaction, the interest rate, which § 1026.36(d)(1) forbids.
notes.explanation: The commentary names the interest rate among the terms on which pay may not be based.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: disclosure does not cure term-based pay. C is wrong: the percentage applies only when the rate is higher, so the rate drives it. D is wrong: the rule covers employees and brokers alike.
notes.evidence: The rule prohibits compensation to a loan originator for a transaction based on, among other things, that transaction's interest rate, annual percentage rate, collateral type

notes.front: May a loan originator be paid differently on different transactions?
notes.back: Yes, provided the difference is not based on a term of a transaction or a proxy for one.
notes.explanation: Variation itself is not forbidden; only term-based variation is.
notes.evidence: Section 1026.36(d)(1) does not prohibit compensating a loan originator differently on different transactions, provided the difference is not based on a term of a transaction or a proxy for a term of a transaction.

notes.front: A consumer pays a mortgage broker a $3,000 fee directly. The creditor also offers the broker a $1,000 payment on the same loan. What does Regulation Z say?
notes.choices:
A) The creditor may not pay the broker; once the consumer pays directly, others may not
B) The creditor may pay if it discloses the payment
C) The creditor may pay up to the consumer's fee
D) The broker may take both if the total is reasonable
notes.back: A) The creditor may not pay the broker; once the consumer pays directly, others may not.
notes.explanation: A person who knows of the consumer-paid compensation may not pay a loan originator in that transaction.
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D all allow a second payer, which the dual compensation ban forbids regardless of disclosure or amount.
notes.evidence: (2) No person who knows or has reason to know of the consumer-paid compensation to the loan originator (other than the consumer) shall pay any compensation to a loan originator, directly or indirectly, in connection with the transaction.

notes.front: A broker firm is paid directly by the consumer. May it pay its own individual loan originator on that loan?
notes.back: Yes, subject to the ban on term-based pay.
notes.explanation: This exception lets consumer-paid firms still pay their staff.
notes.evidence: If a loan originator organization receives compensation directly from a consumer in connection with a transaction, the loan originator organization may pay compensation to an individual loan originator, and the individual loan originator may receive compensation from the loan originator organization, subject to paragraph (d)(1) of this section.

notes.front: Under the anti-steering safe harbour, must the options presented include the loan with the lowest interest rate?
notes.back: Yes, for each type of transaction in which the consumer expressed an interest.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the loan options listed in § 1026.36(e)(3)(i).
notes.evidence: (A) The loan with the lowest interest rate;

notes.front: Which safe-harbour option excludes features such as negative amortisation, a prepayment penalty and interest-only payments?
notes.back: The loan with the lowest interest rate without those risky features.
notes.explanation: The list of excluded features also covers a balloon payment in the first 7 years, a demand feature, and shared equity or appreciation.
notes.evidence: (B) The loan with the lowest interest rate without negative amortization, a prepayment penalty, interest-only payments, a balloon payment in the first 7 years of the life of the loan, a demand feature, shared equity, or shared appreciation;

notes.front: Which safe-harbour option is measured in dollars rather than by rate?
notes.back: The loan with the lowest total dollar amount of discount points, origination points or origination fees.
notes.explanation: Where loans tie on that amount, the one with the lowest interest rate is presented.
notes.evidence: (C) The loan with the lowest total dollar amount of discount points, origination points or origination fees (or, if two or more loans have the same total dollar amount of discount points, origination points or origination fees, the loan with the lowest interest rate

notes.front: Where must a loan originator obtain the loan options it presents under the safe harbour?
notes.back: From a significant number of the creditors it regularly does business with.
notes.explanation: The options must come from a significant number of those regular creditors, not just one.
notes.evidence: The loan originator must obtain loan options from a significant number of the creditors with which the originator regularly does business

notes.front: A broker presents only the one loan that pays him the largest fee, though cheaper loans from his regular lenders suit the consumer. What is the best description?
notes.choices:
A) Fine, because the consumer can refuse
B) Fine, because brokers may choose any lender
C) Dual compensation
D) Likely steering: he may not direct the consumer to a loan for his greater pay unless it is in her interest
notes.back: D) Likely steering: he may not direct the consumer to a loan for his greater pay unless it is in her interest.
notes.explanation: Presenting the three safe-harbour options would have shown compliance; directing her for higher pay does not.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B ignore the steering ban. C concerns being paid by both consumer and others, which is not described.
notes.evidence: a loan originator shall not direct or "steer" a consumer to consummate a transaction based on the fact that the originator will receive greater compensation from the creditor in that transaction than in other transactions

notes.front: What must a loan originator for dwelling-secured consumer credit be, where state or federal law requires it?
notes.back: Registered and licensed under those laws, including the federal mortgage licensing statute and state implementing law.
notes.explanation: The federal statute is the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act of 2008.
notes.evidence: A loan originator for a consumer credit transaction secured by a dwelling must, when required by applicable State or Federal law, be registered and licensed in accordance with those laws, including the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act of 2008

notes.front: A loan originator firm hires an individual who must be licensed under state law. When may he start taking applications?
notes.back: Only once he is licensed or registered as required; the firm must ensure this before he acts as a loan originator.
notes.explanation: The duty rests on the organisation for each individual who works for it.
notes.evidence: Ensure that each individual loan originator who works for the loan originator organization is licensed or registered to the extent the individual is required to be licensed or registered under the SAFE Act,

notes.front: Which names and registry identifiers must a loan originator organisation put on loan documents?
notes.back: Its own name and registry identifier, and the name and identifier of the individual originator primarily responsible.
notes.explanation: The identifier comes from the Nationwide Mortgage Licensing System and Registry, if it has issued one.
notes.evidence: (ii) The name of the individual loan originator (as the name appears in the NMLSR) with primary responsibility for the origination and, if the NMLSR has provided such person an NMLSR ID, that NMLSR ID.

notes.front: A loan originator organisation is preparing a closing package. On which of these must the names and registry identifiers appear: the note, the security instrument, and the credit application?
notes.back: All three.
notes.explanation: The note is one of the documents listed in § 1026.36(g)(2).
notes.evidence: (iii) The note or loan contract; and

notes.front: The first ATR factor is the consumer's current or reasonably expected {{c1::income or assets}}, other than the value of the dwelling securing the loan.
notes.explanation: The home securing the loan cannot itself be counted as the means of repayment.
notes.evidence: (i) The consumer's current or reasonably expected income or assets, other than the value of the dwelling, including any real property attached to the dwelling, that secures the loan;

notes.front: When must a creditor consider the consumer's current employment status under the ATR rule?
notes.back: When it relies on income from the consumer's employment to judge repayment ability.
notes.explanation: If employment income is not relied on, this factor falls away.
notes.evidence: (ii) If the creditor relies on income from the consumer's employment in determining repayment ability, the consumer's current employment status;

notes.front: An ATR factor is the consumer's {{c1::monthly payment on the covered transaction}}, calculated under § 1026.43(c)(5).
notes.explanation: The rule prescribes how that payment is calculated.
notes.evidence: (iii) The consumer's monthly payment on the covered transaction, calculated in accordance with paragraph (c)(5) of this section;

notes.front: Which ATR factor covers a second loan made at the same time?
notes.back: The monthly payment on any simultaneous loan the creditor knows or has reason to know will be made.
notes.explanation: Its payment is calculated under § 1026.43(c)(6).
notes.evidence: (iv) The consumer's monthly payment on any simultaneous loan that the creditor knows or has reason to know will be made, calculated in accordance with paragraph (c)(6) of this section;

notes.front: An ATR factor is the consumer's monthly payment for {{c1::mortgage-related obligations}}.
notes.explanation: The rule lists it separately from the payment on the loan itself.
notes.evidence: (v) The consumer's monthly payment for mortgage-related obligations;

notes.front: Which ATR factor covers what the consumer already owes to others?
notes.back: Current debt obligations, alimony and child support.
notes.explanation: These ongoing obligations reduce what is left to repay the new loan.
notes.evidence: (vi) The consumer's current debt obligations, alimony, and child support;

notes.front: An ATR factor is the consumer's monthly debt-to-income ratio or {{c1::residual income}}.
notes.explanation: Either measure is calculated under § 1026.43(c)(7).
notes.evidence: (vii) The consumer's monthly debt-to-income ratio or residual income in accordance with paragraph (c)(7) of this section; and

notes.front: What is the eighth and last ATR factor?
notes.back: The consumer's credit history.
notes.explanation: It closes the list of eight factors in § 1026.43(c)(2).
notes.evidence: (viii) The consumer's credit history.

notes.front: An underwriter approves a home loan because the house is worth far more than the loan, without checking the borrower's income or debts. Does this meet the ATR rule?
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because the collateral covers the loan
B) Yes, if the loan is below the property value
C) No. Income or assets other than the dwelling's value, and the other factors, must be considered
D) Yes, if the borrower signs a statement of income
notes.back: C) No. Income or assets other than the dwelling's value, and the other factors, must be considered.
notes.explanation: The rule excludes the value of the dwelling securing the loan from the income-or-assets factor.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B rely on the dwelling's value, which the factor excludes. D is wrong: the creditor must consider the factors itself, not rely on a bare statement.
notes.evidence: (i) The consumer's current or reasonably expected income or assets, other than the value of the dwelling, including any real property attached to the dwelling, that secures the loan;

notes.front: By when must the creditor make its ability-to-repay determination?
notes.back: At or before consummation.
notes.explanation: The Bureau's guide adds that the rule applies to a covered mortgage loan.
notes.evidence: The ATR/QM Rule requires a creditor to make a reasonable and good-faith determination of a consumer’s ability to repay at or before consummation of a covered mortgage loan.
notes.source: CFPB, Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage Rule: Small Entity Compliance Guide (version 3.1, April 2021), PDF page 13

notes.front: A general qualified mortgage is not a higher-priced covered transaction. How does it stand under the ATR rule?
notes.back: It complies with the repayment ability requirements: a safe harbour.
notes.explanation: The safe harbour covers general qualified mortgages that are not higher-priced covered transactions.
notes.evidence: A creditor or assignee of a qualified mortgage complies with the repayment ability requirements of paragraph (c) of this section if:

notes.front: A general qualified mortgage is also a higher-priced covered transaction. What protection does the creditor get?
notes.back: A presumption of compliance with the ATR requirements, which can be rebutted.
notes.explanation: Being higher-priced turns the protection into a presumption rather than a safe harbour.
notes.evidence: is presumed to comply with the repayment ability requirements of paragraph (c) of this section.

notes.front: May a general qualified mortgage have payments that increase the principal balance?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Its regular periodic payments must not result in an increase of the principal balance.
notes.evidence: (A) Result in an increase of the principal balance;

notes.front: May a general qualified mortgage let the consumer defer repayment of principal, as interest-only payments do?
notes.back: No, except as § 1026.43(f) allows.
notes.explanation: The payment conditions bar deferral of principal.
notes.evidence: (B) Allow the consumer to defer repayment of principal, except as provided in paragraph (f) of this section; or

notes.front: May a general qualified mortgage end in a balloon payment?
notes.back: No, except as § 1026.43(f) allows.
notes.explanation: The general definition excludes balloons; § 1026.43(f) is the exception.
notes.evidence: (C) Result in a balloon payment, as defined in § 1026.18(s)(5)(i), except as provided in paragraph (f) of this section;

notes.front: A general qualified mortgage must have a loan term that does not exceed {{c1::30 years}}.
notes.explanation: A 40-year term therefore rules out general QM status.
notes.evidence: (ii) For which the loan term does not exceed 30 years;

notes.front: Which of these loans can be a general qualified mortgage, all else being equal?
notes.choices:
A) A 40-year fixed-rate loan
B) A 30-year fixed-rate loan with fully amortising payments
C) A 10-year interest-only loan
D) A loan whose payments do not cover the interest, so the balance grows
notes.back: B) A 30-year fixed-rate loan with fully amortising payments.
notes.explanation: It avoids the barred features: negative amortisation, deferred principal, balloon payments and terms over 30 years.
notes.choicesExplained: A exceeds 30 years. C defers principal. D has negative amortisation.
notes.evidence: (ii) For which the loan term does not exceed 30 years;

notes.front: For a loan amount of $100,000 or more (indexed for inflation), a qualified mortgage's total points and fees may not exceed {{c1::3 percent}} of the total loan amount.
notes.explanation: Smaller loans have their own dollar or percentage limits, and all figures are adjusted each year.
notes.evidence: (A) For a loan amount greater than or equal to $100,000 (indexed for inflation): 3 percent of the total loan amount;

notes.front: A $300,000 loan (well above the indexed threshold) has $10,500 in points and fees. Can it be a qualified mortgage?
notes.back: No. 3 percent of $300,000 is $9,000, and $10,500 exceeds that.
notes.explanation: Over the cap, the transaction is not a qualified mortgage.
notes.evidence: a covered transaction is not a qualified mortgage unless the transaction's total points and fees, as defined in § 1026.32(b)(1), do not exceed:

notes.front: How long after consummation may a permitted prepayment penalty on a covered transaction apply?
notes.back: It must not apply after the three-year period following consummation.
notes.explanation: Within those three years, the amount is also capped as a percentage of the balance prepaid.
notes.evidence: (i) Must not apply after the three-year period following consummation; and

notes.front: If a creditor offers a covered transaction with a prepayment penalty, what must it also offer?
notes.back: An alternative covered transaction without a prepayment penalty.
notes.explanation: The alternative must meet conditions such as the same loan term.
notes.evidence: A creditor must not offer a consumer a covered transaction with a prepayment penalty unless the creditor also offers the consumer an alternative covered transaction without a prepayment penalty

notes.front: What does § 1026.42(c)(1) forbid in a covered transaction?
notes.back: Causing, or trying to cause, the home's value to rest on anything but the valuer's independent judgment, through coercion, bribery, instruction and the like.
notes.explanation: The ban covers direct and indirect attempts by any covered person.
notes.evidence: no covered person shall or shall attempt to directly or indirectly cause the value assigned to the consumer's principal dwelling to be based on any factor other than the independent judgment of a person that prepares valuations, through coercion, extortion, inducement, bribery, or intimidation of, compensation or instruction to,

notes.front: A loan officer tells an appraiser, 'We'll keep sending you work as long as this comes in at $450,000 or more.' Is that a violation?
notes.back: Yes. Implying that future retention depends on the value reported is a listed example of coercion.
notes.explanation: The example targets pressure applied through the appraiser's future work.
notes.evidence: (C) Implying to a person that prepares valuations that current or future retention of the person depends on the amount at which the person estimates the value of the consumer's principal dwelling;

notes.front: A lender asks the appraiser to consider three more comparable sales before finalising the report. Is that a violation?
notes.back: No. Asking the valuer to consider additional, appropriate property information, such as comparable sales, is permitted.
notes.explanation: The information may be used to make or to support a valuation.
notes.evidence: (i) Asking a person that prepares a valuation to consider additional, appropriate property information, including information about comparable properties, to make or support a valuation;

notes.front: For a first-lien loan within the Freddie Mac limit, what APR margins over APOR make it an HPML and a high-cost mortgage?
notes.back: HPML: 1.5 points or more. High-cost mortgage: more than 6.5 points.
notes.explanation: The same loan can be an HPML without being a high-cost mortgage.
notes.contrast: HPML flags moderately high pricing; the high-cost test is reached only at much higher pricing.
notes.evidence: (A) 6.5 percentage points for a first-lien transaction, other than as described in paragraph (a)(1)(i)(B) of this section;

notes.front: How does meeting the general ATR standard differ from making a qualified mortgage?
notes.back: General ATR: the creditor considers the eight factors itself. QM: meeting the QM criteria earns a presumption of ATR compliance.
notes.explanation: Both are routes to complying with the same ability-to-repay requirement.
notes.contrast: Two roads to one rule: prove the underwriting, or fit the QM mould.
notes.evidence: A creditor complies with this ATR requirement if the creditor satisfies the Rule’s general ATR standard when originating a loan.
notes.source: CFPB, Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage Rule: Small Entity Compliance Guide (version 3.1, April 2021), PDF page 13
